sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Separate named sessions and curated memory make Claude work
sections.para: A practical guide from a year of daily use: one session per topic, named project and task, with agents as focused sessions carrying a role.md. Memory is what a session reads, so curate it; vaults let agents share without broad permissions, and review becomes the quality step. Tips and starter prompts follow.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: One topic per session, curated memory, policies before connectors
sections.para: Every recurring topic gets its own named session, and agent sessions get an @ name. An agent is a session with project documents and a role.md. Memory is what the session reads, kept open by default, and vaults carry keys instead of broad permissions, with mistakes traced to briefs and policies written before connectors.

sections.label: One session per topic
sections.line: Mixed-topic threads make the model blend projects together
sections.para: Keep sessions separate, one per major or recurring topic, sometimes in its own tab or window. A thread is the model's frame of reference, so three projects in one thread lead it to borrow names, decisions and assumptions across them. When the topic changes, open a new session.

sections.label: Name every session
sections.line: Name sessions by project and task; prefix agents @
sections.para: A session you cannot find gets recreated badly. The pattern is the project, a pipe and the work, such as sgit.ai | website development. Agent sessions get an @ before the role, like @briefs or @librarian, which signals a defined job and matches how agents refer to each other.

sections.label: What an agent is
sections.line: An agent is a focused session with a role.md
sections.para: An agent is a Claude session with project documents explaining what it is and where it is going, a role.md setting responsibilities and limits, and a name for the role. That is enough to start. The fuller version is in The agent team as it runs and Replicating the agentic inbox.

sections.label: Memory is what the session reads, so curate it
sections.line: Curated memory drives quality and turns review into QA
sections.para: A session's memory is what it reads, so quality comes from curating it. My memory is a set of sites, graphs and vaults wired together from llms.txt. With context that tight, mistakes trace to a brief or missing file, fixed at the source, and Claude should be asked to check facts against sources.

sections.label: Access by default
sections.line: Access by default makes sharing with agents nearly free
sections.para: Almost everything I do is published, mainly for efficiency: anyone, or their agent, can read the latest on the sites. The principle underneath is access by default, not public by default. Inside a company most content can be open to most people, with private material in keyed encrypted vaults.

sections.label: Vaults: how agents receive and send information
sections.line: Vaults let agents exchange files through keys, not permissions
sections.para: Websites send information out; vaults move it between agents and people. One agent writes a brief, another writes its result beside it, and I read both. Sharing means handing over a vault key, soon a key pair, so an agent can do only what that key allows, and a read key gives read-only access.

sections.label: Starter prompts
sections.line: Four reusable prompts open, brief, hand over and close
sections.para: The starter prompts cover opening a project session by reading llms.txt and confirming before work. They also cover starting an agent from its role.md and behaviour policy, handing over a vault key without ever printing or storing it, and ending with a list of changes, checks and doubts plus a debrief for the next session.

sections.label: Tips
sections.line: Previews, prototypes, careful skills and policies before connectors
sections.para: Ask for rendered documents and small proof-of-concept sites, which review better than chat. Read skills before enabling them, and write an Agent Behaviour Policy before every connector, which makes connecting more comfortable. Run one Cowork session per agent, and prefer curating memory directly over Claude or ChatGPT projects.

sections.label: Where to start
sections.line: Split threads first, then add roles, vaults and policies
sections.para: Today, close mixed threads and name one session per topic. This week, write a role.md and open an @ session. Then make memory findable, share through vaults, write a policy before each connector, and fix the brief or file behind any mistake, not only the text.
